newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Oil storage still offers growth prospects - Ommeren.
newsitem.headline: Oil storage still offers growth prospects - Ommeren.

text.p: Oil storage still offers growth potential, even outside Asia, despite the adoption of low stocks policies and pressure on margins, Dutch shipping and tank storage firm Van Ommeren said on Thursday.

Long-term contracts will persist as national governments continue to keep strategic stocks and the oil and petrochemical industry will need distribution channels, while in Europe changes in the market will create new spot opportunities, said executive board member Rick van Westenbrugge.
"In Europe, there will be instances we can benefit from. For example, there will be new mismatches between demand and supply as refineries are closed," he said.
He said refinery closures and the growing trade of products into and out of Russia would provide more permanent opportunies.

Temporary opportunities would result during supply disruptions, such as the likely time lag between the closure of the Leunawerke refinery and the opening of the new Leuna 2000 refinery in eastern Germany later this year.
"In Sweden there is also talk of dismantling their nuclear power stations. They will need their energy from some source. Perhaps there is a chance there," he added.
In the United States, prospects for growth appear more limited, although distribution and importing needs would ensure profitable oil storage businesses.
"In the U.S. the market will grow. Products need to be imported. However, there seems little need for new terminals," Van Westenbrugge said.
His comments came during Van Ommeren's presentation of 1996 results which showed the considerable weakness of the oil storage market.
Van Ommeren's profits for tank storage, including chemicals and vegetable oils, declined from 91.6 million guilders in 1995 to 83.7 million in 1996.
Europe/Africa profit declined by nine percent and in America by 22 percent. In New York, dominated by spot oil trading business, profits suffered.
Van Ommeren said the European market showed "unmistakable signs of saturation", adding "substantial" spare capacity exerted strong pressure on rates.
Van Ommeren itself was also at an advantage compared with rivals because it has a high proportion of long term contracts, which have insulated it from volatile product prices.
Even in the growing Asian market, price competition allowed profits to rise by only five percent.
However, Van Ommeren said the price pressure was likely to be temporary and said demand for oil products, and hence storage, would continue to outstrip the supply from new refineries.

"There are a number of new refineries, but our impression is that the imbalance between demand and supply will be strong in the future. The erosion of tariffs is just a temporary phenomenon," Van Westenbrugge said.

The comments came during Van Ommeren's presentation of full year results. The company posted 1996 net profit of 94.4 million guilders, up from 1995's 80.3 million. The dividend was raised to 2.50 guilders per share from 2.00 in 1995.
